title: Show relationships
summary: Express cause, consequence, contrast, qualification and sequence explicitly with structures that match the evidence rather than decorative linking words.

sections.title: Name the relationship before choosing the connector
content: A connector cannot create logic that the ideas do not contain. Before adding one, state the relationship in plain language: this happened because of that; this result followed; these facts differ; this claim is limited; or these events occurred in this order. Then choose a grammatical structure that makes that exact relationship visible.

E8.2 used relationships to guide sentence structure. E8.3 examines the relationships themselves. The goal is not to collect impressive linking phrases; it is to prevent the reader from guessing how one claim connects to the next.

sections.title: Separate cause from consequence
content: Cause answers why: ‘Because queues were longest during the first ten minutes of lunch, the school opened a temporary second refill point.’ Consequence answers what followed: ‘The second point shared the demand; as a result, the recorded wait at the original station fell during the trial.’ The evidence must support both the event and the claimed link.

Use ‘because’ or ‘since’ before a clause and ‘because of’ before a noun phrase. Use ‘therefore’, ‘as a result’ or ‘consequently’ only when the preceding evidence justifies a consequence. These words do not prove causation by themselves.

sections.title: Distinguish contrast from concession
content: Contrast places different facts beside one another: ‘Thirty-five users found refilling easier, whereas nine reported no difference.’ Concession acknowledges a fact that might weaken or complicate the main point: ‘Although most respondents found refilling easier, the survey did not measure long-term habits.’

Mark the relationship once. ‘Although most respondents approved, but the trial was short’ uses two competing markers. Write either ‘Although most respondents approved, the trial was short’ or ‘Most respondents approved, but the trial was short.’ Use ‘despite’ before a noun phrase, not a complete clause: ‘despite the positive responses’.

sections.title: Qualify the exact boundary of a claim
content: Qualification states where a conclusion stops. Useful limits name the measured place, group, period or outcome: ‘at the original station’, ‘among the 48 surveyed users’, ‘during the one-week trial’ and ‘did not measure total water consumption’. These phrases make a claim more trustworthy, not weaker.

Avoid empty caution such as ‘maybe it was possibly quite successful’. Attach the limit to the claim it controls: ‘The shorter recorded wait suggests that the temporary point eased the lunchtime queue during the trial; it does not establish a lasting change in drinking habits.’

sections.title: Keep sequence separate from causation
content: Sequence tells when events occurred: before, when, during, after and later. An event occurring after another does not by itself prove that the first caused the second. ‘After the second point opened, the recorded wait fell’ reports order. A causal conclusion also needs a credible mechanism, comparison and limits.

When evidence is incomplete, preserve the observation and reduce the claim: ‘The fall occurred during the week in which the second point operated, which is consistent with reduced congestion, although the short trial cannot establish a long-term effect.’ Do not hide uncertainty behind a confident ‘therefore’.

sections.title: Audit logic and grammar together
content: Use four checks. Relationship: does the connector name the real link? Evidence: is that link supported at the strength claimed? Grammar: does the structure fit the marker, such as a clause after ‘although’ or a noun phrase after ‘despite’? Punctuation: are sentence connectors such as ‘however’ separated from the preceding independent clause by a full stop or semicolon?

Classify failures as wrong relationship, unsupported causation, missing qualification, doubled marker, structure mismatch or punctuation fault. Repair the reasoning first; punctuation alone cannot rescue an inaccurate link.

sections.title: Make the logic visible and proportionate
content: Edit a water-refill pilot paragraph from verified notes. Make six decisions about cause, consequence, contrast, concession, qualification and the limit between sequence and causation. Complete the group before viewing feedback.
